label: Economy & Banking
blurb: Central banking, the budget and the institutions that run Indian economic policy. Definitions first, because that is what the paper tests.

topics.title: The Reserve Bank, the Monetary Policy Committee and the rates that matter
topics.hook: One bank, six rates, a six-member committee and an inflation target written into law in 2016.
topics.story:
The **Reserve Bank of India** was established under the **RBI Act 1934** and began operations on **1 April 1935**, on the recommendation of the **Hilton Young Commission** of 1926. It was nationalised on 1 January 1949. Headquarters are in **Mumbai**; the first Governor was **Sir Osborne Smith** and the first Indian Governor **C.D. Deshmukh**.

The **Monetary Policy Committee** was created by the Finance Act 2016 amending the RBI Act, following the **Urjit Patel Committee** report. It has **six members**: three from the RBI, including the Governor as chair and a Deputy Governor, and three appointed by the central government for four years. Decisions are by majority; the **Governor has a casting vote** in a tie. It must meet at least four times a year and in practice meets six times, every two months.

The **inflation target** is **4% CPI**, with a tolerance band of **plus or minus 2%**, set by the government in consultation with the RBI for five years at a time. If average inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must write a report to the government explaining the failure, which happened in 2022.

The rates:
- **Repo rate**: the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks against government securities. The policy rate.
- **Reverse repo**: the rate at which banks park funds with the RBI. Now largely replaced in practice by the **Standing Deposit Facility**, introduced in April 2022, which needs no collateral.
- **Marginal Standing Facility**: emergency overnight borrowing, usually 25 basis points above repo.
- **Bank rate**: the long-term lending rate, aligned with the MSF, used for penal purposes.
- **Cash Reserve Ratio**: the share of net demand and time liabilities banks must keep as cash with the RBI, earning no interest.
- **Statutory Liquidity Ratio**: the share they must hold in cash, gold or approved securities with themselves.

Raising repo, CRR or SLR tightens liquidity and is contractionary. **Open market operations** are the RBI buying or selling government securities to adjust liquidity. The RBI is the **lender of last resort**, the banker to government, the manager of foreign exchange under **FEMA 1999**, and the issuer of currency, except the one rupee note and all coins, which are issued by the **Ministry of Finance**.

facts.v: Six; the Governor chairs and has a casting vote
The Ministry of Finance, not the RBI

topics.why: Passages on inflation or a rate decision expect you to know which rate is the policy rate, how many members the MPC has, and the 4% target with its band.

topics.title: The Union Budget: the deficits, the funds and the constitutional articles
topics.hook: Three deficits that are easy to confuse, three government funds that are easier to confuse, and one date that moved in 2017.
topics.story:
The Budget is the **Annual Financial Statement** under **Article 112**. Since 2017 it is presented on **1 February**, moved from the end of February, and the separate railway budget was merged into it the same year, ending a practice begun in 1924 on the Acworth Committee's recommendation. The first budget of independent India was presented by **R.K. Shanmukham Chetty** on 26 November 1947.

**The three deficits.**
- **Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings. It is the government's total borrowing requirement, and the headline number.
- **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Borrowing to meet running costs.
- **Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit minus interest payments. It shows the current year's imbalance stripped of the legacy of past borrowing.
- **Effective revenue deficit** = revenue deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets, introduced in 2011-12.

**The three funds.**
- **Consolidated Fund of India, Article 266(1)**: all revenues, loans raised and repayments. No money can be withdrawn without parliamentary appropriation.
- **Public Account, Article 266(2)**: money where the government acts as a banker, such as provident funds and small savings. Withdrawals need no appropriation.
- **Contingency Fund, Article 267**: held by the President for unforeseen expenditure, corpus of ₹30,000 crore, recouped later from the Consolidated Fund.

Other articles: **Article 113** on demands for grants, **Article 114** on the Appropriation Bill, **Article 265**, no tax without authority of law, **Article 266**, **Article 280** on the Finance Commission, and **Article 148** on the CAG who audits it all.

The **FRBM Act 2003** set fiscal targets; the current framework follows the **N.K. Singh Committee** recommendation of a debt-to-GDP anchor, 40% for the Centre and 60% general government. The **escape clause** was invoked during the pandemic.

Terms that recur: **vote on account** covers expenditure for a short period pending the full budget; **interim budget** is the full statement presented before an election year; **guillotine** is the Speaker putting all outstanding demands to vote; **cut motions** are policy, economy and token; **capital expenditure** creates assets while **revenue expenditure** does not.

facts.v: Total expenditure minus receipts excluding borrowings

facts.k: No tax without authority of law

facts.v: 2003; N.K. Singh Committee recommended a debt-to-GDP anchor

topics.why: Budget passages test deficit definitions and fund articles rather than numbers. The reliable trap is primary deficit against revenue deficit.

topics.title: Taxation: direct, indirect, and how GST rearranged everything
topics.hook: One tax replaced seventeen, needed a constitutional amendment to exist, and is run by a council where the Centre alone cannot pass anything.
topics.story:
**Direct taxes** are paid by the person on whom they are levied and cannot be passed on: income tax, corporate tax, capital gains tax. The **Central Board of Direct Taxes** administers them. **Indirect taxes** are collected from one person but borne by another, chiefly the consumer: GST, customs duty, excise on the few goods still outside GST. The **Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs** administers those. India has historically collected more from indirect taxes, which are **regressive** because they fall on consumption regardless of income, while direct taxes are **progressive**.

**GST** came into force on **1 July 2017**, enabled by the **101st Constitutional Amendment (2016)**, which inserted **Article 246A** giving both Parliament and state legislatures concurrent power to tax goods and services, **Article 269A** on inter-state supply, and **Article 279A** creating the **GST Council**. It subsumed central excise, service tax, additional customs duties, state VAT, entry tax, luxury tax, entertainment tax and octroi. Outside GST: petroleum crude, petrol, diesel, aviation turbine fuel, natural gas, alcohol for human consumption, electricity and stamp duty.

**The GST Council** is chaired by the Union Finance Minister, with the Union Minister of State for Finance and one minister from each state. Decisions need a **three-fourths weighted majority**, with the Centre holding one third of the weight and all states together two thirds, so neither side can act alone. In *Mohit Minerals* (2022) the Supreme Court held that Council recommendations are **persuasive, not binding**, since both Union and states have simultaneous legislative power.

**Structure.** Four main slabs, 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%, with special rates of 0.25% on rough diamonds and 3% on gold, and a compensation cess on demerit and luxury goods. **CGST** and **SGST** are levied together on intra-state supply; **IGST** on inter-state supply and imports, collected by the Centre and apportioned. GST is a **destination-based consumption tax**, so revenue accrues where the good is consumed, not where it is produced, which is why manufacturing states resisted it.

Other terms: **cess** is a tax for a specific purpose and is not shareable with states; **surcharge** is a tax on tax, also not shared, which is why the states object when the Centre leans on both. **Laffer curve**, **ad valorem**, **specific duty** and **tax buoyancy** recur in passages.

facts.v: One third; states together two thirds
Persuasive, not binding, per Mohit Minerals, 2022
Petroleum products, alcohol for human consumption, electricity, stamp duty

topics.why: A passage on state finances or a Council meeting will test the voting weights and whether recommendations bind. The classic recall question is which goods stayed outside GST.

topics.title: Measuring the economy: GDP, inflation and the indices that rank India
topics.hook: Six measures of national income, two measures of inflation, and about a dozen international indices whose publisher is the question.
topics.story:
**National income.** **GDP** is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year. **GNP** is GDP plus net factor income from abroad. **NDP** is GDP minus depreciation; **NNP** is GNP minus depreciation, and **NNP at factor cost** is **national income**. **Per capita income** is national income divided by population. **Nominal** figures use current prices; **real** figures use constant prices from a base year, currently **2011-12** in India. The ratio of nominal to real GDP is the **GDP deflator**, the broadest measure of inflation. Estimates are produced by the **National Statistical Office** under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.

**Inflation.** The **Consumer Price Index** measures retail prices and is the RBI's target; food carries a large weight, which is why Indian CPI swings with monsoons. The **Wholesale Price Index**, compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser in the Ministry of Commerce, excludes services entirely and no longer anchors policy. Types worth naming: **demand-pull**, from excess demand; **cost-push**, from rising input costs; **stagflation**, high inflation with stagnant growth and high unemployment; **deflation**, a general fall in prices; **disinflation**, a fall in the rate of inflation; **reflation**; and **skewflation**, a price rise in one or a small group of commodities, a term coined in India for food inflation.

**Indices and who publishes them.**
- **Human Development Index**, UNDP, since 1990, devised by **Mahbub ul Haq** with **Amartya Sen**. Life expectancy, education and gross national income per capita.
- **Global Hunger Index**, Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe. India has disputed its methodology.
- **World Happiness Report**, UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network.
- **Corruption Perceptions Index**, Transparency International.
- **Press Freedom Index**, Reporters Without Borders.
- **Global Innovation Index**, WIPO.
- **Environmental Performance Index**, Yale and Columbia.
- **Global Gender Gap Report**, World Economic Forum.
- **Ease of Doing Business**, formerly World Bank, discontinued in 2021 after data irregularities and being replaced by B-READY.
- **Multidimensional Poverty Index**, UNDP with the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative; NITI Aayog publishes an Indian version.

facts.v: Value of final goods and services produced within the borders
GDP plus net factor income from abroad
Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce
Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen
Discontinued by the World Bank in 2021

topics.why: Index-to-publisher matching is asked directly and is easy marks. The concept trap is GDP against GNP, and stagflation against deflation.

topics.title: The banking system: nationalisation, bad loans and the regulators
topics.hook: Fourteen banks nationalised in one night in 1969, a bankruptcy code in 2016 that finally let lenders take a company away from its promoter, and four regulators who keep colliding.
topics.story:
**Nationalisation.** The **Imperial Bank of India** became the **State Bank of India** in 1955 after the Gorwala Committee. On **19 July 1969**, Indira Gandhi nationalised **14 banks** with deposits above ₹50 crore, through an ordinance later replaced by an Act; the ordinance was struck down in *R.C. Cooper v. Union of India* (1970) for inadequate compensation, and Parliament re-enacted it. Six more were nationalised in **1980**. Public sector banks have since been merged repeatedly, most heavily in 2020, leaving twelve.

**Structure.** Scheduled commercial banks are those in the **Second Schedule of the RBI Act 1934**, which requires paid-up capital and reserves of at least ₹5 lakh. Categories: public sector, private sector, foreign, regional rural banks (created 1975 on the Narasimham Committee's recommendation), small finance banks and payments banks (both from 2015 guidelines, with payments banks barred from lending). Co-operative banks are dual-regulated by the RBI and state registrars, a weakness exposed by the PMC Bank collapse and addressed by the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act 2020.

**Bad loans.** A **non-performing asset** is a loan where interest or principal has been overdue for **90 days**. Classification runs sub-standard, doubtful, loss. The RBI's **Asset Quality Review of 2015** forced banks to recognise what they had been evergreening. Tools to recover: the **SARFAESI Act 2002**, which lets secured creditors seize collateral without a court; **Debt Recovery Tribunals** under the 1993 Act; and the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016**, which created a time-bound process of 180 days extendable to 330, run by a resolution professional under the **Committee of Creditors**, with **operational creditors** ranking below financial creditors in the waterfall under section 53. The **IBBI** regulates it. Section 29A bars defaulting promoters from bidding for their own companies.

**Regulators.** **RBI** for banks and payments; **SEBI**, statutory since 1992, for securities; **IRDAI** for insurance, headquartered in Hyderabad; **PFRDA** for pensions. **Deposit insurance** is provided by the **DICGC**, a wholly owned RBI subsidiary, covering **₹5 lakh** per depositor per bank, raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020.

facts.v: R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, 1970

topics.why: Expect a passage on a bank failure or a resolution under the IBC. The reliable questions are the 90-day NPA rule, the ₹5 lakh insurance cover and the 1969 date.

topics.title: The external sector: balance of payments, reserves and trade rules
topics.hook: A current account that runs a deficit, a capital account that funds it, and a set of trade rules India argues with every year at Geneva.
topics.story:
The **balance of payments** records all transactions between residents and the rest of the world. It has two parts. The **current account** covers trade in goods, trade in services, primary income (interest and dividends) and secondary income (remittances). The **capital and financial account** covers foreign direct investment, portfolio investment, loans and banking capital. The two must balance, with errors and omissions closing the gap; reserve movements are the residual.

India runs a **merchandise trade deficit** and a **services surplus**, and receives the world's **largest inflow of remittances**, over 100 billion dollars a year. The net result is a current account deficit funded by capital inflows. The **CAD as a share of GDP** is the number that gets quoted; anything beyond about 3% is treated as a warning sign, as in the taper tantrum of 2013.

**FDI versus FPI.** Foreign direct investment involves a lasting management interest, conventionally 10% or more of equity, and is stable. Foreign portfolio investment is financial, liquid and quick to leave, which is why it is called hot money. India's FDI comes through the **automatic route** for most sectors and the **government route** for sensitive ones; since April 2020 all investment from countries sharing a land border with India requires government approval. Sectors with caps: multi-brand retail 51%, insurance 74%, print media 26%; defence allows 74% automatic and more by approval.

**Reserves** are held by the RBI in foreign currency assets, gold, Special Drawing Rights and the reserve tranche position at the IMF. **SDRs** are the IMF's reserve asset, valued on a basket of five currencies: US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen and pound sterling; the renminbi entered in 2016.

**Trade rules.** The **WTO** was created on **1 January 1995** by the **Marrakesh Agreement**, replacing the **GATT** of 1947, after the **Uruguay Round**. Headquarters in Geneva; decisions are by consensus, one country one vote. Key agreements: **TRIPS** on intellectual property, **TRIMS** on investment measures, **GATS** on services, and the **Agreement on Agriculture**, whose rules on public stockholding for food security India has fought over since the Bali Ministerial of 2013, where it secured a **peace clause**. The **Appellate Body** has been paralysed since 2019 because the United States has blocked appointments.

facts.v: Goods, services, primary and secondary income
India, over 100 billion dollars a year
Government approval required for all investment from neighbours, since April 2020
US dollar, euro, renminbi, yen, pound sterling

topics.title: From the Planning Commission to NITI Aayog
topics.hook: A body with no constitutional or statutory basis directed India's investment for sixty-five years, and was abolished by a press release.
topics.story:
The **Planning Commission** was set up by a **Cabinet resolution in March 1950**. It was neither a constitutional body nor a statutory one, and its authority came from the Prime Minister chairing it and from its control over the allocation of plan funds to states. The **National Development Council**, created in 1952 and including all Chief Ministers, formally approved the plans.

Twelve **Five Year Plans** ran from 1951 to 2017. The **First (1951-56)** followed the Harrod-Domar model and put agriculture first after Partition; it met its target. The **Second (1956-61)**, built on the **Mahalanobis model**, chose heavy industry and public sector capital goods, and the **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956** gave the state the commanding heights. The **Third** was broken by the wars of 1962 and 1965 and the drought that followed, and three **annual plans**, the plan holiday, ran from 1966 to 1969, the years of devaluation and the beginnings of the **Green Revolution**. The **Fourth** aimed at growth with stability and self-reliance; the **Fifth** carried **garibi hatao**, was cut short by the Janata government, and the **Sixth** dropped the Nehruvian frame. The **Eighth (1992-97)** was the first after the **1991 liberalisation**, and turned the state from a producer into a facilitator. The **Twelfth (2012-17)**, targeting faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth, was the last.

**NITI Aayog**, the National Institution for Transforming India, replaced the Commission on **1 January 2015**, again by resolution. It does not allocate funds; that moved to the Finance Ministry, which mattered because the **Fourteenth Finance Commission** had raised the states' share of the divisible pool from 32% to 42% at the same time. NITI's stated role is cooperative and competitive federalism, and it works largely through indices and advice: the **SDG India Index**, the **Multidimensional Poverty Index**, the composite water and health indices, and the **Aspirational Districts Programme**. It is chaired by the Prime Minister, with a Vice Chairman, a Chief Executive Officer and a Governing Council of all Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors.

facts.v: Set up by Cabinet resolution, March 1950; neither constitutional nor statutory

passages.title: The tax that needed an amendment
passages.passage:
The tax introduced in July 2017 could not have been enacted by ordinary legislation. Under the constitutional scheme as it then stood, the power to tax the manufacture of goods lay with the Union and the power to tax their sale lay with the states, and neither could trespass on the other. Merging the two into a single levy therefore required a constitutional amendment, which created a new article giving both levels of government simultaneous power over the same tax base for the first time.

The amendment also created a council in which the Union and the states negotiate the rates. Its voting rules are unusual. A decision requires three quarters of the weighted votes cast. The Union holds one third of the weight and all the states together hold two thirds. The arithmetic means the Union cannot carry a proposal alone, since a third falls short of three quarters, and the states cannot carry one alone either, since two thirds also falls short. Every decision needs the Union and a substantial majority of states together.

For five years after the tax came into force, states were guaranteed compensation for any shortfall against a notional fourteen per cent annual growth in their revenue from the taxes they had surrendered, funded by a cess on luxury and demerit goods. The guarantee expired in 2022; the cess did not, having been extended to service the loans taken to pay the compensation during the pandemic.

In 2022 the Supreme Court held that the council's recommendations are persuasive rather than binding. Since both Parliament and the state legislatures hold the taxing power simultaneously, the Court reasoned, neither is subordinate to a body that merely recommends. The judgment unsettled an assumption that had governed the system since its inception, though in practice the council has continued to work by consensus.

Several goods were left outside the new tax altogether. Petroleum products and alcohol for human consumption remained with the states, which is why fuel prices still vary from one state to the next.

questions.q: The new article created by the amendment, giving both levels simultaneous power, is:
questions.explain: Article 246A. Article 269A deals with inter-state supply and Article 279A creates the GST Council; Article 246 is the original division of powers under the Seventh Schedule.

questions.q: On the voting arithmetic described in the second paragraph, which is correct?
options: The Union can carry a proposal alone
The states together can carry a proposal alone
Neither side can carry a proposal without the other
A simple majority of members suffices
questions.explain: Three quarters is required. One third and two thirds each fall short of three quarters, so the Union and a substantial majority of states must agree together.

questions.q: The 2022 judgment referred to in the fourth paragraph is:
options: Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan
questions.explain: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) held GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding, because both Union and states hold simultaneous legislative power.

questions.q: Why do fuel prices still vary between states, on the passage?
options: Fuel is taxed at different GST slabs
Petroleum products were kept outside the new tax
Fuel is taxed only by the Union
questions.explain: Petroleum crude, petrol, diesel, ATF and natural gas were kept outside GST, so state VAT and excise continue to apply at differing rates.

questions.q: The compensation guarantee described in the third paragraph was based on assumed annual revenue growth of:
questions.explain: Fourteen per cent a year against a 2015-16 base, guaranteed for five years from 1 July 2017 and funded by the compensation cess.

passages.title: Targeting inflation
passages.passage:
Until 2016 the central bank pursued several goals at once and was never told in law which one mattered most. An amendment to its governing statute that year gave it a single primary objective, price stability, while adding that growth was to be kept in view. The government was to notify a numerical target once every five years in consultation with the bank; the figure chosen was four per cent, with a band of two percentage points on either side. It was renotified without change at the end of the first cycle.

The target is set on the consumer price index, not the wholesale index that had earlier dominated commentary. The choice matters because food and fuel carry much more weight in what households buy than in what factories pay for, so the two series can diverge for months. The bank publishes a measure that strips out those two volatile groups when it wants to describe underlying pressure.

Rates are no longer set by the Governor alone. A committee of six decides, three from the bank and three appointed by the government for four-year terms, and each member has one vote. Ties are broken by the Governor's casting vote. The committee meets at least four times a year, its decisions are published the same day, and the minutes with each member's statement follow a fortnight later.

Failure is defined rather than left to argument. If average inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the bank must send the government a report explaining why it happened, what it proposes to do, and how long it expects the correction to take. That report is not made public. The obligation was triggered for the first time in 2022, after supply shocks pushed prices above the upper bound.

questions.q: The inflation target notified under the framework is:
questions.explain: Four per cent with a tolerance band of two percentage points, so between two and six per cent.

questions.q: The target is measured on:
questions.explain: Headline CPI combined. Core inflation, which excludes food and fuel, is watched but is not the target.

questions.q: The Monetary Policy Committee has:
options: Four members, all from the RBI
Six members, three from the RBI
Eight members, four from the RBI
questions.explain: Six: the Governor, a Deputy Governor, one officer nominated by the Board, and three external members appointed by the central government.

questions.q: A tie in the committee is resolved by:
options: A fresh vote at the next meeting
Reference to the Union Finance Minister
questions.explain: The Governor has a second, casting vote in addition to a regular one.

questions.q: The framework treats the target as breached when inflation stays outside the band for:
questions.explain: Three consecutive quarters, which obliges the RBI to report to the central government on the causes and the remedial action.

passages.title: Planning without a statute
passages.passage:
The body that directed where India's public investment went for sixty-five years was created by a resolution of the cabinet in March 1950. No article of the Constitution mentions it and no Act of Parliament established it. Its authority came from two things: the head of government chaired it, and it decided how much of the central pool each state received for its plan projects. A separate council of all state chief executives formally approved each plan, which gave the arrangement a federal appearance without giving the states much leverage.

The first plan leaned on a growth model relating output to the rate of saving and investment, put agriculture first because Partition had cut the country off from its main irrigated wheat and jute areas, and met its target. The second took a different route entirely, following a statistician's four-sector model that argued a poor country should build the industries that build machines, even at the cost of consumption in the short run. A policy resolution the same year reserved the strategic sectors to the state. That choice defined the next three decades.

Then the sequence broke. Two wars and a severe drought forced three annual plans in place of a five-year one, and the devaluation and food imports of those years are still argued about. Growth returned but so did the balance of payments, and by the time the eighth plan was written the crisis of 1991 had already changed the state's role from producer to referee.

The commission was replaced in January 2015, again by resolution rather than statute. The successor advises and publishes indices but does not hand out money; the transfer function moved to the finance ministry, at the same moment as a finance commission raised the states' untied share of central taxes by ten percentage points.

questions.q: The body described was created by:
questions.explain: The Planning Commission was set up by a Cabinet resolution in March 1950.

questions.q: The model behind the second plan is associated with:
questions.explain: The Mahalanobis four-sector model, favouring capital goods industries.

questions.q: The council of state chief executives that approved plans was the:
questions.explain: The National Development Council, created in 1952.

questions.q: The three annual plans of 1966 to 1969 are known as the:
questions.explain: The plan holiday, forced by two wars and drought.

questions.q: On the passage, the successor body differs most importantly in that it:
questions.explain: NITI Aayog advises and publishes; allocation moved to the Finance Ministry.

passages.title: One tax, thirty-one legislatures
passages.passage:
Before 2017 a manufactured good crossing India could attract excise from the centre, value added tax from each state, an entry tax from a municipality, a central sales tax that the exporting state kept, and a cascade of levies on levies that nobody could compute exactly. The reform took seventeen years from the first committee report, and it required something no ordinary statute could deliver: every state surrendering the power to tax the sale of goods, and the centre surrendering the power to tax their manufacture, simultaneously.

The instrument was a constitutional amendment in 2016. It inserted a new article creating a council of the union finance minister and one minister from every state, and gave both Parliament and the state legislatures concurrent power to make laws on the new tax, with the centre alone empowered to levy it on inter-state supply and to apportion the proceeds. Voting in the council was weighted so that neither side could act alone: three-quarters of the votes cast are needed, the centre holds a third and the states two-thirds between them.

The design carries two features that trouble constitutional lawyers. The first is that the tax is destination-based, so revenue accrues where the goods are consumed rather than where they are made, which shifted money from manufacturing states to populous consuming ones and required a compensation guarantee, originally for five years, funded by a cess. The second is the status of the council's word. It was assumed to bind until the Supreme Court held in 2022, in a case about integrated tax on ocean freight, that its recommendations are persuasive only, since both Parliament and the state legislatures possess simultaneous legislative power and neither can be reduced to an executor of another body's decisions.

That ruling did not cause the system to unravel, and the council's recommendations continue to be adopted. What it did was restate what the amendment had actually done, which was to create a forum for negotiated federalism rather than a supra-legislature.

questions.q: The council was created by:
questions.explain: Article 279A, inserted by the 101st Amendment.

questions.q: Voting in the council requires:
questions.explain: Three-fourths of weighted votes cast, with the centre holding one-third.

questions.q: The tax is destination-based, which means revenue accrues:
questions.explain: Which is why manufacturing states required a compensation guarantee.

questions.q: The 2022 judgment held that the council's recommendations are:
questions.explain: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals held them persuasive, given simultaneous legislative power.

questions.q: On the passage, the reason the reform needed a constitutional amendment was that:
options: Both centre and states had to surrender existing taxing powers
questions.explain: The simultaneous surrender of powers could not be done by ordinary statute.
